lead: An LED, a seven-segment display and an LCD are output devices that a microcontroller drives through GPIO pins. Each needs a safe current and correct signal timing. A keypad is many switches sharing few pins; the CPU scans rows and columns to find the pressed key. These parts appear in appliances, meters, medical panels and project boards: a microwave shows time on a seven-segment or LCD, and a door lock reads a 4×4 keypad. The sections below give the resistor calculation, display drive levels, LCD handshake and keypad scan.
prereq: You need: 3.1 GPIO and I/O ports and 3.2 timers for multiplexing.

blocks.text: An LED is a diode that emits light when forward biased. Its forward voltage V<sub>f</sub> is the drop across it when lit, and I<sub>f</sub> is the rated current. A GPIO pin gives a source voltage V<sub>s</sub>, usually 3.3 V or 5 V. A series resistor R limits the current. If the resistor is too small, the LED and pin overheat; if too large, the LED is dim.

blocks.where: R is the series resistance in ohms (Ω); V<sub>s</sub> is the supply or pin voltage in volts (V); V<sub>f</sub> is the LED forward voltage in volts; I<sub>f</sub> is the wanted forward current in amperes (A). Convert mA to A by dividing by 1000.

blocks.text: A seven-segment display is seven LEDs named a to g, plus a decimal point. In a common-cathode part all cathodes join ground; drive a segment anode high to light it. In a common-anode part all anodes join V<sub>cc</sub>; drive a segment cathode low to light it. The drive levels are opposite, so read the part number before writing code.

Multiplexing drives one digit at a time. A timer turns on digit 1, waits about 1 ms to 5 ms, turns it off, then turns on digit 2. If the whole display refreshes faster than about 50 Hz, the eye sees all digits on because of persistence of vision. Use one series resistor per segment, not one in the common line, to keep brightness even.

A character LCD has a controller and a parallel bus. RS selects instruction register when 0 and data register when 1. RW selects write when 0 and read when 1. E is the enable strobe. D0–D7 carry a byte, or D4–D7 carry two nibbles in 4-bit mode. To write, set RS and RW, put the byte on the data bus, then pulse E high and low. The controller samples the bus on the falling edge.

Before sending characters, initialize: wait for power-up, function set (8-bit or 4-bit, lines, font), display off, clear display, entry mode, display on. After each command, read the busy flag: RS=0, RW=1; D7=1 means busy. Wait until D7=0. If you do not check busy, commands can be lost.

A 16×2 module has two lines of 16 characters. Address the first line from 0x00 and the second from 0x40 in the common controller map. Send the address as a command, then send data bytes. Keep the E pulse within the module's timing; a slow GPIO toggle is usually safe, a very fast one is not.

A 4×4 keypad has 16 push buttons in four rows and four columns. Rows R0–R3 are outputs; columns C0–C3 are inputs with pull-up resistors. A pull-up holds a floating input at 1. With no key pressed, all columns read 1. A pressed key connects its row to its column.

items: Drive all rows high; wait for lines to settle.
Drive row R0 low, keep R1–R3 high; read C0–C3.
If a column reads 0, the key at that row and column is pressed.
Repeat for R1, R2, R3; then repeat the whole scan.
After a 0 is seen, wait 10 ms to 20 ms and read again; accept the key only if it is still 0. This is debounce.

blocks.text: Ghosting happens when three keys form an L shape: the unpressed fourth corner can also read 0. Use diodes in series with each key, or scan one key at a time, or accept only one key. Debounce stops one physical press from becoming many key events. A timer interrupt can call the scan every 5 ms to 10 ms.

One scan step: R2 is driven low. The columns read C0=1, C1=0, C2=1, C3=1. The 0 is at column 1, so the key is at row 2, column 1. With labels left to right, top to bottom from 1, key number = row×4 + column + 1 = 2×4 + 1 + 1 = 10. The figure shows this cell.

figure.caption: A 4×4 keypad matrix with rows R0–R3 and columns C0–C3. Row R2 is driven low; the marked cell at column C1 reads 0, so key 10 is pressed.

spec.title: 4x4 keypad matrix
spec.aria: A 4 by 4 keypad matrix with rows R0 to R3 and keys 1 to 16; key 10 at row R2 column C1 is marked.

examples.question: A red LED has V<sub>f</sub> = 2.0 V and needs I<sub>f</sub> = 10 mA from a 5 V GPIO pin. Find the series resistor and the nearest standard value (use 330 Ω). A 4×4 keypad has rows R0–R3 as outputs and columns C0–C3 as inputs with pull-ups. R2 is driven low; the columns read C0=1, C1=0, C2=1, C3=1. Which key is pressed if labels run left to right, top to bottom from 1?
steps: Use R = (V<sub>s</sub> − V<sub>f</sub>) / I<sub>f</sub> = (5 V − 2.0 V) / 0.010 A = 3.0 V / 0.010 A = 300 Ω.
The nearest listed standard value is 330 Ω. A 300 Ω resistor is not a common E12 value.
Keypad: row index is 2 for R2. The only 0 is at C1, so column index is 1.
examples.answer: The resistor is 300 Ω; use the standard 330 Ω. The pressed key is key 10.
examples.check:
Vs = 5.0
Vf = 2.0
If = 0.010
R = (Vs - Vf) / If
standard = 330
row = 2
col = 1
key = row * 4 + col + 1
print(int(R))
print(standard)
print(key)

traps: Common-anode and common-cathode seven-segment displays need opposite drive levels; using the wrong one lights all or no segments.
A keypad input without a pull-up floats; it may read random keys. Enable internal pull-ups or add external resistors.
No debounce gives multiple key events for one press; a 10 ms to 20 ms recheck fixes most switches.
Check the LCD busy flag before the next command; a fixed delay alone can fail at some temperatures and voltages.
The LED resistor formula uses current in A, not mA; using 10 instead of 0.010 gives 0.3 Ω.

quiz.q: What does the RS signal do on a character LCD?
quiz.a: RS=0 selects the instruction register; RS=1 selects the data register.

quiz.q: Why does a keypad column input need a pull-up?
quiz.a: With no key, the input would float. The pull-up holds it at 1; a pressed key connects it to a low row and reads 0.

quiz.q: A red LED has Vf=2.0 V and needs 12 mA from 5 V. Find the series resistor and the standard 270 Ω choice.
quiz.a: 12 mA = 0.012 A. R = (5−2)/0.012 = 250 Ω. Use the standard 270 Ω resistor.

quiz.q: R2 is low; columns read C0=0, C1=1, C2=1, C3=0. Which keys could be pressed if labels run left to right, top to bottom from 1?
quiz.a: Row 2 has keys 9, 10, 11, 12. C0=0 gives key 9; C3=0 gives key 12. Two keys in the same row are pressed.

quiz.q: An LCD busy-flag read has RS=0, RW=1 and D7=1. What should the program do?
quiz.a: Wait and poll again. D7=1 means the controller is busy; send the next command only when D7=0.

quiz.q: Why use multiplexing on a seven-segment display?
quiz.a: It shares segment lines among digits, reducing pin count; fast refresh gives persistence of vision.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern products often replace parallel character LCDs with I2C or SPI OLED/TFT modules, and keypads with capacitive touch or GPIO expanders. Search 'HD44780 busy flag timing', 'keypad debounce state machine', 'char LCD I2C backpack', and 'touch keypad controller'. In safety panels, keypad ghosting and stuck-key detection become formal requirements.
